---
title: "Probit: a normal latent variable and Fisher scoring"
jupyter: python3

## 1. Simulated observations

We observe **simulated students**, with study hours, a practice score and a
binary pass/fail outcome. The column of ones estimates an intercept. R seed 20261013 generates 120
students: hours are uniform between 1 and 12, scores are clipped to 20–95 from
45 + 3 × hours + normal noise with standard deviation 8. Both are rounded to two decimals.

The underlying simulation is a **latent normal threshold** model:

$$z_i^*=-1.9+0.13\,\mathrm{hours}_i+0.011\,\mathrm{score}_i+\epsilon_i,
\quad \epsilon_i\sim N(0,1),\quad y_i=\mathbf{1}\{z_i^*>0\}.$$

With $\eta_i=x_i^\top\beta$, symmetry of the standard normal gives
$P(y_i=1)=P(\epsilon_i>-\eta_i)=\Phi(\eta_i)$. The latent value is a model
construction: only the resulting 0 or 1 is supplied to the estimator. Fixing the
latent variance to one identifies the coefficient scale; there is no sigma to estimate.

The normal CDF $\Phi(a)$ is the area under a standard-normal density to the left
of $a$. The density is $\phi(a)=e^{-a^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}$, and $\Phi'(a)=\phi(a)$.
Unlike a logit coefficient, $e^{\beta_j}$ is **not** a constant odds multiplier.
The local probability slope is $\phi(\eta_i)\beta_j$, so it varies by observation.

The hand-worked iteration below starts from zero coefficients so the first
weights and dot products are easy to inspect. phit also starts from zero, except
for extreme inputs with a ones column, where it uses a finite marginal intercept
start. Starting values change the iteration path, not the likelihood or the
converged estimates.

```{python}
from pathlib import Path
import json
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from scipy.special import ndtr, log_ndtr, gammaln, xlogy
from scipy.stats import norm
from IPython.display import Math, display
ROOT = next(p for p in [Path.cwd(), *Path.cwd().parents] if (p / "Cargo.toml").exists())
observations = pd.read_csv(ROOT / "docs/data/probit-learning.csv")
X = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(observations)), observations[['study_hours', 'practice_score']]])
y = observations.iloc[:,-1].to_numpy(dtype=float)
n,p = X.shape
fixture = json.loads((ROOT / "tests/fixtures/probit-r.json").read_text())
case = next(c for c in fixture["cases"] if c["name"] == "simulated_learning")
np.testing.assert_array_equal(X,case["x"])
np.testing.assert_array_equal(y,case["y"])
display(observations.head(8))
display(observations.corr().rename_axis("Sample correlations"))
def number(value):
    text = f"{value:.6g}"
    if "e" in text:
        mantissa, exponent = text.split("e")
        return mantissa + rf"\times10^{{{int(exponent)}}}"
    return text

def show_matrix(symbol, values, limit=6):
    matrix = np.asarray(values)
    if matrix.ndim == 1:
        matrix = matrix[:, None]
    indices = list(range(len(matrix))) if len(matrix) <= limit else [0,1,2,None,len(matrix)-1]
    columns = list(range(matrix.shape[1])) if matrix.shape[1] <= limit else [0,1,2,None,matrix.shape[1]-1]
    rows = [" & ".join(r"\ddots" if j is None else r"\vdots" for j in columns) if i is None
            else " & ".join(r"\cdots" if j is None else number(matrix[i,j]) for j in columns) for i in indices]
    display(Math(symbol + r"=\begin{bmatrix}" + r" \\ ".join(rows)
                 + r"\end{bmatrix}" + rf"\quad({matrix.shape[0]}\times{matrix.shape[1]})"))

def show_dot(symbol, left, right):
    terms = [rf"({number(a)})\cdot({number(b)})" for a,b in zip(left,right)]
    if len(terms) > 3:
        terms = terms[:2] + [r"\cdots", terms[-1]]
    display(Math(symbol + "=" + "+".join(terms) + r"\approx" + number(np.asarray(left) @ right)))


show_matrix("X",X)
show_matrix("y",y)
show_matrix(r"X^\top",X.T)
```

Matrix displays show dimensions and truncate middle rows/columns using dots.
Calculations use every observation and full precision. Correlation does not
establish causation. The saved dataset is shared by the PHP example and R fixtures;
regeneration is explicit in `tests/generate-probit-poisson-fixtures.R`.

## 2. Likelihood and derivatives

For independent Bernoulli outcomes the log-likelihood is

$$\ell(\beta)=\sum_i[y_i\log\Phi(\eta_i)+(1-y_i)\log\Phi(-\eta_i)].$$

The complement is written $\Phi(-\eta)$ to avoid subtracting a CDF rounded to one.
Taking a derivative with respect to $\eta_i$ gives

$$s_i=\phi(\eta_i)\frac{y_i-\pi_i}{\pi_i(1-\pi_i)},\qquad
\pi_i=\Phi(\eta_i),\qquad g=X^\top s.$$

For a success this is $\phi/\Phi(\eta)$; for a failure it is
$-\phi/\Phi(-\eta)$. These ratios are evaluated from log density minus log tail
probability. Rust uses `erfc` for ordinary tails and a normal Mills-ratio continued
fraction beyond -8, preserving finite log-likelihoods even when the CDF underflows.

Expected negative curvature, or **Fisher information**, is

$$I=X^\top W X,\qquad
w_i=\frac{\phi(\eta_i)^2}{\pi_i(1-\pi_i)}.$$

One way to see this is to square $s_i$ and take its expectation:
$E[(y_i-\pi_i)^2]=\pi_i(1-\pi_i)$, leaving the expression above.
Unlike canonical logistic regression, observed curvature and expected information
need not agree at a finite probit sample. We use Fisher scoring and its covariance,
matching R glm and statsmodels GLM; a discrete-model probit fit's observed-Hessian
covariance can differ without either calculation being erroneous.

## 3. Scoring, weighted matrices and SVD

Fisher scoring solves $I\Delta\beta=g$ and updates coefficients. For probit
this is not Newton's method, because expected information differs from the
observed negative Hessian (section 2). To avoid
forming and inverting the cross-product for fitting, define column scales $D$,
$A=XD^{-1}$ and $\theta=D\beta$. Solve

$$B\Delta\theta\approx q,\quad B=W^{1/2}A,\quad q=W^{-1/2}s,
\qquad B=USV^\top,\quad \Delta\theta=VS^{-1}U^\top q.$$

The weighted least-squares normal equations are
$A^\top W A\Delta\theta=A^\top s$. This is the same update in scaled coordinates,
with $\Delta\beta=D^{-1}\Delta\theta$. We display cross-products to understand
them; the production solve uses weighted SVD. See the [OLS SVD explanation](ols-math.qmd#what-problem-does-svd-help-us-understand).

Weights and scores change each iteration: this is IRLS. The full increment can
overshoot, so a decreasing-likelihood step is halved, at most 30 times. Both a
small full coefficient increment and a small likelihood change are required.
A tiny damped step alone does not establish convergence; the limit is 100 updates.

```{python}
def values(eta):
    log_density = -0.5*eta**2-0.5*np.log(2*np.pi)
    probability = ndtr(eta)
    root = np.exp(log_density-0.5*(log_ndtr(eta)+log_ndtr(-eta)))
    score = np.where(y == 1, np.exp(log_density-log_ndtr(eta)), -np.exp(log_density-log_ndtr(-eta)))
    return probability,root,score

def log_likelihood(eta):
    return np.where(y == 1,log_ndtr(eta),log_ndtr(-eta)).sum()

scales = np.linalg.norm(X,axis=0)
A = X/scales
theta = np.zeros(p)
history=[]
for iteration in range(1,101):
    eta=A@theta
    fitted,root,score=values(eta)
    B=root[:,None]*A
    q=score/root
    U,singular,Vt=np.linalg.svd(B,full_matrices=False)
    assert np.all(singular > np.finfo(float).eps*max(n,p)*singular[0])
    step=Vt.T@((U.T@q)/singular)
    old_ll=log_likelihood(eta)
    fraction=1.0
    for _ in range(31):
        candidate=theta+fraction*step
        new_ll=log_likelihood(A@candidate)
        if np.isfinite(new_ll) and new_ll >= old_ll-16*np.finfo(float).eps*(1+abs(old_ll)): break
        fraction/=2
    else: raise RuntimeError("No improving step")
    if iteration==1:
        show_matrix(r"\beta^{(0)}",theta/scales)
        show_matrix(r"s^{(0)}",score)
        show_matrix(r"W^{(0)}_{1:5,1:5}\text{ (top-left block)}",np.diag(root[:5]**2))
        show_matrix(r"g^{(0)}=X^\top s",X.T@score)
        show_matrix(r"I^{(0)}=X^\top W X",X.T@(root[:,None]**2*X))
        for j in range(p): show_dot(rf"g_{{{j+1}}}",X[:,j],score)
        show_dot(r"I_{2,3}",X[:,1],root**2*X[:,2])
        show_matrix("B",B)
        show_matrix("q",q)
        show_matrix(r"U^\top q",U.T@q)
        show_matrix(r"\Delta\beta",step/scales)
    history.append({"iteration":iteration,"fraction":fraction,"log-likelihood":new_ll,
                    "intercept":candidate[0]/scales[0],"predictor 1":candidate[1]/scales[1],"predictor 2":candidate[2]/scales[2]})
    small=np.all(np.abs(step)<=1e-11*(1+np.abs(candidate)))
    small_ll=abs(new_ll-old_ll)<=1e-13*(1+abs(old_ll))
    theta=candidate
    if small and small_ll: break
else: raise RuntimeError("Did not converge")
beta=theta/scales
eta=X@beta
fitted,root,score=values(eta)
display(pd.DataFrame(history))
show_matrix(r"\hat\beta",beta)
show_matrix(r"X^\top s\text{ at final fit}",X.T@score)
show_dot(r"\hat\eta_1",X[0],beta)
print("First fitted probability:",fitted[0])
```

Starting coefficients are zero. They imply probability 0.5 and weights $2/\pi$ (about 0.63662) for every observation.
These are starting guesses, not the observed predictors or outcomes.
The first displayed gradient is a set of actual data dot products.

## 4. Covariance and Wald inference

Evaluate information at the final coefficients, then compute

$$\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\hat\beta)=I(\hat\beta)^{-1},\quad
\operatorname{SE}_j=\sqrt{\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\hat\beta)_{jj}},\quad
z_j=\hat\beta_j/\operatorname{SE}_j.$$

The SVD supplies the covariance as $D^{-1}VS^{-2}V^\top D^{-1}$.
Two-sided p-values use $2P(Z\ge |z_j|)$ and 95% Wald limits use
$\hat\beta_j\pm1.959964\operatorname{SE}_j$. These are asymptotic normal tests,
not OLS Student t tests. We do not multiply covariance by RSS/(n-p).
R `confint.default()` supplies equivalent Wald intervals; ordinary GLM `confint()`
uses profile likelihood instead.

```{python}
_,singular,Vt=np.linalg.svd(root[:,None]*A,full_matrices=False)
covariance=((Vt.T/singular)@(Vt/singular[:,None]))/scales[:,None]/scales[None,:]
se=np.sqrt(np.diag(covariance))
z=beta/se
p_values=2*norm.sf(np.abs(z))
conf_int=np.column_stack([beta-norm.ppf(.975)*se,beta+norm.ppf(.975)*se])
show_matrix(r"\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\hat\beta)",covariance)
show_matrix(r"\hat\mu\text{ or }\hat\pi",fitted)
display(pd.DataFrame({"coefficient":beta,"SE":se,"z":z,"p":p_values,"95% lower":conf_int[:,0],"95% upper":conf_int[:,1]},index=["intercept",*observations.columns[:2]]))
display(pd.DataFrame({"observed":y,"fitted":fitted,"response residual":y-fitted}).head(8))
```

## 5. Likelihood, deviance and AIC

For individual binary outcomes the saturated likelihood is zero, giving
$D=-2\ell(\hat\beta)$. The intercept-only null probability is the observed success
proportion. Without a ones column, the null baseline is 0.5. Neither a latent
variance nor an OLS residual variance is estimated. A probit coefficient is on
the latent normal scale: multiplying it by a normal density converts it to a local
probability slope, not an odds ratio.

AIC is $2p-2\ell(\hat\beta)$; residual degrees of freedom are $n-p$, without an
estimated dispersion parameter. Predictions are probabilities, and residuals
are observed minus fitted. These vectors follow retained input row order.

```{python}
ll=log_likelihood(eta)
null_ll=np.sum(y*np.log(y.mean())+(1-y)*np.log1p(-y.mean()))
model_deviance=-2*ll
null_deviance=-2*null_ll
print("First local probability slope for predictor 1:",norm.pdf(eta[0])*beta[1])
calculated=dict(coefficients=beta,covariance=covariance,std_errors=se,z_statistics=z,p_values=p_values,
                conf_int=conf_int,fitted=fitted,residuals=y-fitted,log_likelihood=ll,
                deviance=model_deviance,null_deviance=null_deviance,aic=2*p-2*ll,df_residual=n-p)
for key,value in calculated.items():
    np.testing.assert_allclose(value,case["expected"][key],atol=1e-9,rtol=1e-7,err_msg=key)
print({key:calculated[key] for key in ["log_likelihood","deviance","null_deviance","aic","df_residual"]})
print("Every statistical field agrees with the saved R fixture.")
```

## 6. Assumptions, failure modes and experiments

Both observed classes must remain after missing-row deletion. Complete or quasi
separation can make a finite MLE nonexistent; encountered separating directions
are rejected, as are singular information and iteration exhaustion. This certificate
check is not exhaustive separation detection. Near separation can produce poor
Wald inference even for a converged fit. Try replacing passed by study_hours > 6:
what would happen to the latent coefficient as the probabilities approach the labels?

For both methods the retained design must have n > p and full numerical rank.
Missing null/NAN rows are dropped with a warning unless missing: 'raise'. No partial
unconverged result is returned. See the [contract](../contracts.qmd) and the
[executed three-way comparison](https://phit.phpstats.org/verification/probit).

## Rust connections

`fit_probit` owns its input vectors and converts them to nalgebra matrices.
Borrowed matrix operands remain available for later iterations; iterators construct
weights and score residuals. A dedicated loop performs this estimator's updates.
`Result` and `?` propagate validation/numerical failures. The returned struct holds
numeric fields; the PHP binding converts those fields into an associative array
and adds warning/sample metadata. No generic optimizer or family hierarchy is added.
See [Rust learning notes](../ols-math.qmd) and `crates/stats-core/src/probit.rs`.

Reference documentation: [R glm](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/stats/html/glm.html),
[R families](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/stats/html/family.html),
[statsmodels GLM](https://www.statsmodels.org/stable/glm.html).
